accepted_examples.german: Tom ist in etwa so groß wie ich.
accepted_examples.english: Tom is about the same height as me.
accepted_examples.note: groß means large/tall; the sentence compares height.

accepted_examples.german: Was hast du da in der linken Hand?
accepted_examples.english: What's that you have in your left hand?
accepted_examples.note: Hand is the body part used in the literal sense.

accepted_examples.german: Er bewahrte die Ruhe im Angesicht der Gefahr.
accepted_examples.english: He kept calm in the face of the danger.
accepted_examples.note: Ruhe means calm/composure in this context.

accepted_examples.german: Ich weiß nicht, wann Tom angerufen hat, aber es war entweder gestern oder vorgestern.
accepted_examples.english: I don't know when Tom called, but it was either yesterday or the day before.

accepted_examples.german: Was für eine Art von Mädchen bist du?
accepted_examples.english: What kind of girl are you?

accepted_examples.german: Wer hat sich als Letzter eingeloggt?
accepted_examples.english: Who was the last person to log on to the computer?
accepted_examples.note: Letzter is substantivized as the last person.

accepted_examples.german: Er gab zu, den Schatz gestohlen zu haben.
accepted_examples.english: He admitted that he had stolen the treasure.

accepted_examples.german: Nach langem Warten kamen wir endlich hinein.
accepted_examples.english: After a long wait, we finally got in.
accepted_examples.note: endlich means finally/after a long wait.

accepted_examples.german: He, Leute! Es wird spät.
accepted_examples.english: Hey guys, it's getting late.
accepted_examples.note: he is used as an attention-getting interjection.

accepted_examples.german: Es ist zu schwer, um es zu bewegen.
accepted_examples.english: It's too heavy to move.

accepted_examples.german: Kannst du die Länge messen?
accepted_examples.english: Can you measure the length?
accepted_examples.note: messen means to measure a quantity.

accepted_examples.german: Wasser ist für das Leben unverzichtbar.
accepted_examples.english: Water is essential to life.
accepted_examples.note: Wasser means water, the liquid essential for life.

accepted_examples.german: Das erste, was ich sah, war ein Hund.
accepted_examples.english: The first thing I saw was a dog.

accepted_examples.german: Wir denken zu viel und fühlen zu wenig.
accepted_examples.english: We think too much and feel too little.

accepted_examples.german: Es war nett von dir, das zu sagen.
accepted_examples.english: It was nice of you to say that.

accepted_examples.german: Eine Woche hat sieben Tage.
accepted_examples.english: A week has seven days.
accepted_examples.note: Woche means a period of seven days.

accepted_examples.german: Wolltest du deshalb nicht, dass ich komme?
accepted_examples.english: Is this the reason you didn't want me to come?

accepted_examples.german: Welche Vorteile hat es, früh aufzustehen?
accepted_examples.english: What are some of the benefits of waking up early?
accepted_examples.note: welche asks which/what; the English uses some in this construction.

accepted_examples.german: Die Brücke ist sehr lang und sehr hoch.
accepted_examples.english: The bridge is very long and very tall.

accepted_examples.german: Das Alter beschleicht uns, ohn’ dass wir’s bemerken.
accepted_examples.english: Old age creeps upon us unnoticed.

accepted_examples.german: Der Tisch nimmt in diesem Zimmer viel Platz ein.
accepted_examples.english: The table takes up a lot of space in this room.
accepted_examples.note: Zimmer means a room within a building.

accepted_examples.german: Ich stieg in meinen Wagen und ließ den Motor an.
accepted_examples.english: I got in my car and started the motor.
accepted_examples.note: Wagen means car in this context.

accepted_examples.german: Es klingt so, als ob ihr Spaß habt.
accepted_examples.english: It sounds like you're having fun.

accepted_examples.german: Warum wollen Sie niemals über die Vergangenheit reden?
accepted_examples.english: Why don't you ever want to talk about the past?

accepted_examples.german: Du weißt, wie ernst die Lage ist, oder?
accepted_examples.english: You know how serious things are, don't you?

held_examples.german: Das Haus ist bis auf den Grund abgebrannt.
held_examples.reason: This is the idiom 'burned to the ground'; Grund means ground/foundation here, not a property or piece of land.

held_examples.german: Mama sein ist schwerer, als ich dachte.
held_examples.reason: The English translation says parent and loses the specific female-parent meaning of Mama.

held_examples.german: Tom war schon oft allein gewesen, aber an jenem Nachmittage war ihm zum erstenmal richtig einsam zumute.
held_examples.reason: This uses gewesen as the Partizip II of sein, not as the rare adjective meaning former.

held_examples.german: Hast du auch bestimmt die Tür geschlossen?
held_examples.reason: bestimmt functions adverbially as surely/definitely here, not as the adjective certain in this entry.

editorial_examples.german: Das Haus steht auf eigenem Grund und Boden.
editorial_examples.english: The house stands on privately owned land.
editorial_examples.note: This expresses Grund as property/land belonging to an owner.
The translation preserves Mama as a female parent.

editorial_examples.german: Ich bin noch nie in Berlin gewesen.
editorial_examples.english: I have never been to Berlin.
editorial_examples.note: gewesen is the Partizip II of sein in a perfect construction.

editorial_examples.german: Er hat eine bestimmte Vorstellung davon.
editorial_examples.english: He has a certain idea of it.
editorial_examples.note: bestimmte is the inflected adjective meaning specific/certain.

entry_updates.note: Duden identifies gewesen as the Partizip II of sein; the prior 'former' sense was for the homographic rare adjective.
Treat this frequency form as a participle of sein, not as the rare adjective.

entry_updates.value: Partizip II of sein; used with sein to form the perfect, e.g. Ich bin in Berlin gewesen.
entry_updates.note: Replace the adjective-declension note with the correct verb-form note.

entry_updates.value: Not applicable: this entry is the Partizip II of sein.
entry_updates.note: The adjective comparison candidate does not apply to the corrected verb-form entry.

inflected_links.form_note: Partizip II of sein; this is an inflected verb form, not a separate verb lemma.

plural_reviews.note: Both appear as substantivized adjective forms: strong plural Letzte and weak/definite plural die Letzten.

plural_reviews.value: Usually no plural in the history sense; Geschichten means stories.
plural_reviews.note: Duden marks the historical development/discipline senses as singular-only; plural Geschichten belongs to the story sense.
Duden records the plural Alter for the neuter life-age sense.

plural_reviews.value: No plural in the enjoyment/fun sense; Späße means jokes.
plural_reviews.note: Duden marks the enjoyment/fun sense as singular-only; Späße is the plural for the joke sense.
